9.0.s.en: 1. The victories of Alexander the Great:

9.0.0.en: 1 The burden of the word of the LORD in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be the rest thereof. For the LORD has the eye of man and of all the tribes of Israel. 2 And Hamath also shall border thereby; Tyrus, and Zidon, though it be very wise. 3 And Tyrus did build herself a strong hold, and heaped up silver as the dust, and fine gold as the mire of the streets. 4 Behold, the Lord will possess her, and smite her power in the sea; and she shall be devoured with fire. 5 Ashkelon shall see it, and fear; Gaza also shall see it, and be very sorrowful, and Ekron; for her expectation shall be ashamed; and the king shall perish from Gaza, and Ashkelon shall not be inhabited. 6 And a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines. 7 And I will take away his blood out of his mouth, and his abominations from between his teeth: but he that remaineth, even he, shall be for our God, and he shall be as a governor in Judah, and Ekron as a Jebusite. 8 And I will encamp about mine house because of the army that goeth and returneth, so that no collector of tribute shall pass over them any more: for now have I seen with mine eyes.

9.0.1.en: He presents an oracle, a prophecy that carries a threat against the resisting nations and reassurance for those who rely on God.

9.0.2.en: First: Alexander the Great's attitude toward the cities of Syria and Phoenicia: "The burden of the word of the LORD in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be the rest thereof. For the LORD has the eye of man and of all the tribes of Israel. And Hamath also shall border thereby; Tyrus, and Zidon, though it be very wise. And Tyrus did build herself a strong hold, and heaped up silver as the dust, and fine gold as the mire of the streets. Behold, the Lord will possess her, and smite her power in the sea; and she shall be devoured with fire" [1-4].

9.0.3.en: Alexander the Great defeated a number of the cities of Syria, among them Hadrach, which is on the river Orontes not far from Hamath, but his eyes were on Damascus, the capital. The terror and amazement caused by his victories had drawn the eyes of the children of Israel to God, asking divine help from Him. As for Hamath, which is next to Damascus, it fell before him.

9.0.4.en: After Syria, Alexander entered Phoenicia and subdued Tyre, which was very rich through its trade, so that silver was to it like dust and gold like worthless mire; its inhabitants were compelled to fortify themselves on an island opposite Tyre, but Alexander burned the ancient city with fire and cast its stones into the sea to build a causeway by which he crossed to the island and besieged its fortresses, and they collapsed before him.

9.0.5.en: St. Didymus the Blind sees in Damascus and the other lands of Syria a symbolic picture of the nations that resisted the truth and then returned and accepted it, since it is said here: "Behold, the Lord will possess her"... He restores her from her former savagery to gentleness. As for Tyre, with its massive wall in which she fortified herself, it signifies the heretics who fortify themselves with sophistical arguments as their strongholds, but God also works to subject them to the true faith.

9.0.6.en: Tyre in truth represents the man who has become rich (Rev 3:17) and thought that he is able by himself to fortify himself and by his wealth to be satisfied; but as he gathers silver it becomes to him dust, and as he stores gold it becomes to him mire. The word of God, which is silver in itself, is turned to dust for him because of his earthly mind, and the spiritual life, which is heaven in itself, is turned to mire because of his descent to material things. He falls into the sea, which symbolizes the whirlpools of the world and the storms of anxiety and grief, and is devoured by the destroying fire, as sin crushes him and scatters his life and possessions! Wretched is this man who thinks himself very wise, as Tyre thought, and so ruined her silver and gold and cast herself into the sea of the love of the world and the destroying furnace of sin!

9.1.0.en: Second: Alexander's attitude toward the cities of Philistia: "Ashkelon shall see it, and fear; Gaza also shall see it, and be very sorrowful, and Ekron; for her expectation shall be ashamed..." [5]. In this passage and what follows it four Philistine cities are mentioned (Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, Ashdod), and the fifth of the principal cities, "Gath," is not mentioned, perhaps because it had not been rebuilt after it fell at the hand of Uzziah (2 Chr 26:6). Ashkelon feared and Gaza was very sorrowful, and Ekron also, when they saw what had befallen Tyre, the great fortified city, and realized the danger that was coming upon them.

9.1.1.en: These four cities, "Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, Ashdod," signify the world with its four directions, which was filled with the pagan world, haughty, yet it comes back and returns to the Lord the Savior and enjoys salvation. These cities also signify earthly man, bound to the earth (the four quarters of the world), who has returned to his Savior bearing the spiritual mark.

9.1.2.en: "Ashkelon" is a Hebrew word derived from "shekel," that is, weight; "Gaza" means "might" or "strength"; "Ekron" means "barrenness"; "Ashdod" means "stiff, or ravager."

9.1.3.en: So Ashkelon signifies the soul that prides itself on its weight and measure; when the fear of the Lord comes upon it, it realizes itself and returns to the Lord that He may be everything to it, as the Psalmist says that those who fear the Lord "shall not want any good thing" (Ps 34:10).

9.1.4.en: And Gaza is very sorrowful [5]; what she counted might and strength she sees as nothing, so she receives the Lord Himself as her might and strength and inner glory.

9.1.5.en: And Ekron, as she realizes her barrenness, returns in contrition to the Lord her Savior, and He grants her blessed children (spiritual fruits), as the Psalmist says: "He maketh the barren woman to keep house, and to be a joyful mother of children" (Ps 113:9), and as it was said: "so that the barren hath born seven; and she that hath many children is waxed feeble" (1 Sam 2:5). This is the Church of the Gentiles, which was barren and bore many, while the company of the Jews, the possessors of the promises and covenants, among whom were the Fathers and prophets, withered because of its rejection of the Savior. Isaiah the prophet says: "Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear; break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail with child: for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife" (Isa 54:1). And as St. Didymus the Blind says: ["The married wife" (Baal) here is the Law; so the Gentiles, who were without the Law of Moses, were filled with joy at salvation, and the Jews, who had the Law, fell into the spiritual depth.

9.1.6.en: As for "Ashdod," when she realizes her corrupting stiffness and its destructive work she returns to the Lord and becomes subject to Him. Her god Dagon falls before the ark of the covenant (1 Sam 5) and her resistance to the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem ends (Neh 4:7), so that she receives the preaching of the Gospel by Philip (Acts 8:40) and becomes an episcopal see carrying out the preaching of salvation.

9.2.0.en: The prophet speaks of what happens in Ashdod, saying: "And a bastard (illegitimate sons) shall dwell in Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines. And I will take away his blood out of his mouth, and his abominations from between his teeth: but he that remaineth, even he, shall be for our God, and he shall be as a governor in Judah, and Ekron as a Jebusite" [6-7]. This was fulfilled literally, for Ashdod almost lost its native inhabitants, since it was the policy of Alexander the Great to mix the conquered peoples together so as to deprive them of their national feeling. As for taking away the blood from the mouth, it signifies their abandoning idolatry, in which they ate the sacrifices with their blood (Ezek 33:25). The Law prohibited that (Lev 17:10-11; Acts 9:4). Ashdod returned to the Lord by accepting the Christian faith and her original dignity was restored to her, so she became as a governor in Judah, as Ekron, that is, the barren, became as a Jebusite in that she treads the love of the world under her feet.

9.3.0.en: Third: Alexander's attitude toward the Jews: "And I will encamp about mine house because of the army that goeth and returneth, so that no collector of tribute shall pass over them any more: for now have I seen with mine eyes" [8]. The Lord encamped about His house so that the army of Alexander the Great would not touch it in its repeated passing through Jerusalem, for he did not harm the Jews although he humbled the Samaritans. Josephus the Jewish historian mentions that Jaddua the high priest met Alexander with all the priests wearing the holy garments, the high priest wearing the turban on his head and the golden plate on which was written "Holiness to the LORD"; when Alexander saw him he bowed down to him and told him that he had seen in a dream the God whose name was written on the plate, then he entered Jerusalem and offered sacrifices and gave the Jews special privileges.

9.3.1.en: The Lord ends His speech here by saying: "for now have I seen with mine eyes." And as St. Didymus the Blind says: [This clear vision is the power of insight of which the Apostle writes: "all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do" (Heb 4:13)]... as if what the Lord declares through the prophet is uncovered to the Lord, the Planner of our salvation!

9.4.0.en: 9 Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and victorious, and lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass. 10 And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off: and he shall speak peace unto the heathen: and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth. 11 As for thee also, by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water. 12 Turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope: even to day do I declare that I will render double unto thee.

9.4.1.en: Lest some think that Zechariah aims at the salvation of the Macedonian age and the Lord's giving grace to the Jews in the eyes of Alexander, he moves on to the true salvation through the meek King, the Savior, the giver of peace to the world. God's open eyes behold His work of salvation as a present work by which humanity is saved; therefore He says: "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and victorious, and lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass. And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off: and he shall speak peace unto the heathen: and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth" [9-10].

9.4.2.en: A people deprived of its land for a long time and subjected under foreign kings in captivity: behold, its King comes to it, who makes the daughter of Zion rejoice greatly and gladdens the heart of the daughter of Jerusalem. He is a wonderful King, as St. John Chrysostom says: [He does not lead chariots like the rest of kings, nor demand tribute, nor drive people away, nor ask for guards, but walks in His great meekness].

9.4.3.en: We presented previously, in the commentary on the Gospel according to Matthew, the thought of the Fathers of the Church in interpreting this text and the symbols that the colt and the ass carried when the Lord rode them at His entry into Jerusalem, and the symbols that Jerusalem carried in receiving the Lord with rejoicing. And here we notice:

9.4.4.en: First: St. Didymus the Blind sees that the word "Zion" means "observer of the commandments or one who carries them out," while Jerusalem means "vision of peace," as if those who enjoy gladness and exultation at the Lord's entry into their lives are the doers of the commandments and those who enjoy the vision of peace (through the Cross). The Psalmist says: "The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes" (Ps 119:8). "By the first (carrying out the commandment) the soul rejoices greatly at the coming of the true King, and by the second (the vision of peace) she shouts because she is in a very elevated position announcing the coming of the King of kings... The first received a command to rejoice and the second received a command to proclaim it!

9.4.5.en: May we truly be the daughter of Zion and so rejoice greatly through our keeping of the divine commandment, and let us be the daughter of Jerusalem and shout, declaring witness to Him through our vision of the true peace that surpasses all in the crucified Lord!

9.4.6.en: Second: As the meek Lord the Savior enters the heart, He cuts off the war chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem and removes the battle bow, so that peace comes within, and Ephraim becomes fruitful and Jerusalem enjoys true peace, singing: "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God. They are brought down and fallen: but we are risen, and stand upright" (Ps 20:7-8).

9.4.7.en: Third: The dominion of the Lord the King extends over the nations, from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. Perhaps by the seas He means those who used to drink salt water through pagan teachings, while by the river He means the holy Law of Moses, so He brings the Gentiles together with the Jews under His dominion.

9.5.0.en: Fourth: He says: "As for thee also, by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water. Turn you to the strong hold, ye prisoners of hope: even to day do I cry that I will render double unto thee" [11-12]. It seems that Israel, as a company of farmers, each group of them had hewn a pit for themselves among the rocks so that when the time of rain came it would fill with water; so when the time of captivity came and they entered into a state of terror they fled from the enemies to the pit in which there was no water and became prisoners there. Perhaps this pit signifies the human self which man establishes by himself to confine himself in it by himself, but God releases him by the covenant of the holy blood, releases him from his selfishness and his self that he may live in the fullness of the freedom of the Cross. And St. Didymus the Blind sees in this pit without water, into which Joseph and Jeremiah and Daniel, etc., were cast, a sign of Hades, which has no water of eternal life, from which the Lord has released us not through the blood of bulls and goats but through the blood of the New Covenant. He calls us to come out of the pit to go forth to the stronghold, which is the glorious Church without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27). "There the captives drawn out of the pit without water find rest." For in the Church the Lord's prisoners find "a stronghold for uprightness is the way of the LORD" (Prov 10:29), and the Lord Himself is a stronghold: "Be thou to me a rock of refuge, whereunto I may continually resort" (Ps 71:3), "Be thou my strong rock, for an house of defence to save me. For thou art my rock and my fortress; therefore for thy name's sake lead me, and guide me" (Ps 31:2-3).

9.5.1.en: Sixth: God restores to the soul a double reward in place of the days of its toil, and as St. Didymus the Blind says: [He who is a prisoner of Christ settles in this city and sits in the glorious strongholds within it, and lives without fear as he awaits double consolations and encouragement in place of sorrow... The reward will be double for the former afflictions, and the clear example of that is the story of Job, who had a strong soul and so received a double reward (Job 42:11)]. He receives a double reward, as he enjoys a hundredfold in this world and eternal life in the world to come; it is also double since he receives the salvation of the soul together with the body. And the secret of its doubling, as St. Didymus the Blind says: [He who is in captivity, when he returns from his captivity, is not only saved but becomes a teacher of his oppressors, so his glory is doubled glory!]

9.6.0.en: 13 For I have bent Judah for me, filled the bow with Ephraim, and raised up thy sons, O Zion, against thy sons, O Javan, and made thee as the sword of a mighty man. 14 And the LORD shall be seen over them, and his arrow shall go forth as the lightning: and the Lord GOD shall blow the trumpet, and shall go with whirlwinds of the south. 15 The LORD of hosts shall defend them; and they shall devour, and tread upon sling stones; and they shall drink, and make a noise as through wine; and they shall be filled like bowls, and as the corners of the altar. 16 And the LORD their God shall save them in that day as the flock of his people: for they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon his land. 17 For how great is his goodness, and how great is his beauty! corn shall make the young men grow, and new wine the maids.

9.6.1.en: After speaking of the victories of Alexander the Great and how God gave favor to the Jews in his eyes, and then returning to tell us of the Messiah King, he speaks here of "Javan," that is, the Greeks, since the Maccabees defeated them in the second century before the Nativity (Dan 11:32; 8:9-14), and the prophecy came to affirm one thing: that God is the secret of their victory.

9.6.2.en: He says "I have bent Judah for me" [13]; what is this arrow that goes forth from Judah to raise up the sons of Zion against the sons of Javan but the Lord Christ Himself, the divine arrow going forth from the tribe of Judah on behalf of the sons of faith against the devil and his evil works?! He is the word of the living and effective God, sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb 4:12), who says: "he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword" (Isa 49:2).

9.7.0.en: As the arrow was launched on behalf of the salvation of humanity against the devil, the Lord was manifested in His kingdom, and as the prophet says: "And the LORD shall be seen over them, and his arrow shall go forth as the lightning: and the Lord GOD shall blow the trumpet, and shall go with whirlwinds of the south. The LORD of hosts shall defend them" [14-15]. The Lord Christ, the true arrow, has gone forth like lightning; He enters the heart and wounds it with the wounds of love, so that the soul says: "I am sick of love" (Song 5:8); He destroys in it the works of the devil and flashes in it with the splendor of His glory. And as it is written in Habakkuk: "At the light of thine arrows that fly, at the shining of the lightning of thy glory" (Hab 3:11). And as St. Didymus the Blind says: [Jerusalem is Judah... as the divine arrow goes forth from it like lightning, the inner man is enlightened and the eyes of the heart are enlightened]. And as the Lord gives enlightenment to the eyes of the soul by the lightning, so the blowing of the trumpet gives an inner ear to hear His voice that resounds to warn us of the enemy the devil and to join us to the celebration of His joyful coming, since trumpets were sounded at war as at feasts.

9.8.0.en: Thus he prophesies about the victory over the Greeks by the Maccabees, and declares our eternal victory over the devil in Christ Jesus, the true divine arrow. He has depicted this victory for us by saying: "The LORD of hosts shall defend them; and they shall devour, and tread upon sling stones; and they shall drink, and make a noise as through wine; and they shall be filled like bowls, and as the corners of the altar. And the LORD their God shall save them in that day as the flock of his people: for they shall be as the stones of a crown, lifted up as an ensign upon his land. For how great is his goodness, and how great is his beauty! corn shall make the young men grow, and new wine the maids" [15-16].

9.8.1.en: If God used the pagans as sling stones that He aimed at His people to chasten them, then when He returns to them with His mercy He makes these stones beneath them, which they tread with their feet; so in the same thought, if God allows us various trials or afflictions, He uses them for our discipline or our approval, and in His love does not make us fall under the trial, but the trial falls beneath us and has no authority over us to deprive us of our inner peace and our joy in the Lord.

9.8.2.en: And just as at the captivity the people drank the cup of God's wrath with sorrow and pain, so when God has compassion on them they drink the cup of gladness and joy!

9.8.3.en: He gives victory to His people as His rational flock, and sets them up as the stones of a crown lifted up upon His land, and according to the Septuagint He sets them up as holy stones rolling upon the earth. St. Jerome comments on this, saying: [Note His saying: "holy stones rolling upon the earth"; they are wheels that run upon the earth, hastening toward the high places]. He also says: ["A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together" (Eccl 3:5). Now God has raised up from the hard stones of the Gentiles children to Abraham (Mt 3:9), and they have become holy stones rolling upon the earth (Zech 9:16), which have passed through the winnowing fan of the air of the world and rolled in the chariot of God on swift wheels]. And when he spoke of Paula, who spent her money not on stone buildings but on the poor, he said: [She wished to spend her money not on the stones that pass away with the passing of the world but on the living stones that roll upon the earth, and by which the city of the great King is built, as it is said in the Book of Revelation (Rev 21:14)].

9.8.4.en: Through this surpassing victory that lifts the soul to heaven as living stones rolling upward to the Jerusalem above, the soul feels a spiritual satisfaction, for it is said "corn shall make the young men grow, and new wine the maids"... God offers Himself as wheat and new wine to satisfy our young men and young women, that is, to make the fruits of the Spirit grow in us through the sanctification of the soul with all its faculties (the young men) and the body with all its senses and emotions (the maids).
